facts.statement: The genus Vegasaurus contains only one known species, Vegasaurus molyi.
facts.quote: It contains a single species, Vegasaurus molyi.

facts.statement: Vegasaurus is known only from the holotype specimen MLP 93-I-5-1, a nearly complete postcranial skeleton missing the tail tip, housed at the La Plata Museum in Argentina.
facts.quote: Vegasaurus is known solely from the holotype MLP 93-I-5-1, a nearly complete well preserved postcranial skeleton (lacking the tip of the tail) housed at the La Plata Museum in La Plata, Argentina.

facts.statement: The holotype skeleton includes the entire neck with 54 cervical vertebrae, various back and tail vertebrae, girdles, limbs, ribs, and 45 gastroliths found near the dorsal region.
facts.quote: Elements include the whole neck with 54 complete cervical vertebrae, three pectoral vertebrae, 17 back vertebrae, three sacral vertebrae, the front and middle tail vertebrae, pectoral and pelvic girdles, forelimbs and hindlimbs, ribs, and 45 gastroliths associated with the dorsal region.

facts.statement: The holotype was discovered in 1989 by Eduardo Olivero, Daniel Martinioni, Francisco Mussel, and Jorge Lusky at Cape Lamb on Vega Island, the northernmost part of the Antarctic Peninsula.
facts.quote: MLP 93-I-5-1 was discovered in 1989, by Eduardo Olivero, Daniel Martinioni, Francisco Mussel and Jorge Lusky, at Cape Lamb of Vega Island at the edge of the Antarctic Peninsula of James Ross Archipelago (northernmost part of Antarctica).

facts.statement: The specimen was collected from a 3-square-meter area in a semi-articulated state at locality "Assemblage 10" in the early Maastrichtian stage, approximately 72 million years ago.
facts.quote: MLP 93-I-5-1 was collected from an area of 3 square meters in a semi-articulated state, at locality "Assemblage 10", which belongs to the middle section of Cape Lamb Member of the Snow Hill Island Formation, dating to the early Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous, about 72 million years ago.

facts.statement: Vegasaurus was first described and named by José P. O'Gorman, Leonardo Salgado, Eduardo B. Olivero, and Sergio A. Marenssi in 2015.
facts.quote: Vegasaurus was first described and named by José P. O'Gorman, Leonardo Salgado, Eduardo B. Olivero and Sergio A. Marenssi in 2015 and the type species is Vegasaurus molyi.

facts.statement: Vegasaurus is unique among elasmosaurids for having 54 neck vertebrae.
facts.quote: Vegasaurus is unique among elasmosaurids in having 54 neck vertebrae.

facts.statement: Vegasaurus had an estimated body length of 6.15 to 6.5 meters and a body mass of 839 kilograms.
facts.quote: It has an estimated body length of 6.15 - 6.5 m and body mass of 839 kg.

facts.statement: Phylogenetic analysis places Vegasaurus with Morenosaurus and the aristonectines Aristonectes and Kaiwhekea, all Late Cretaceous South Pacific elasmosaurids.
facts.quote: In the resultant topology, Vegasaurus nests with three other Late Cretaceous South Pacific elasmosaurids, being Morenosaurus, and two species from the Weddell Sea region, the aristonectines Aristonectes and Kaiwhekea.

facts.statement: Vegasaurus differs from Aristonectinae by having elongated neck vertebrae, linking it to taxa like Futabasaurus from the other side of the Pacific.
facts.quote: Vegasaurus differs from the two members of Aristonectinae by having elongated neck vertebrae, yet links them to taxa from the other side of the Pacific, e.g. Futabasaurus from Japan.

facts.statement: In the resulting phylogenetic topology, Vegasaurus groups with Morenosaurus and two Weddell Sea genera, the aristonectines Aristonectes and Kaiwhekea.
facts.quote: En la topología resultante, Vegasaurus se aloja junto con otros tres elasmosáuridos cretácicos del Pacífico Sur, los cuales son Morenosaurus y dos géneros de la región del mar de Weddell, los aristonectinos Aristonectes y Kaiwhekea.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen shows a pathological bone callus on a rib indicating a fracture that occurred while the animal was healing.
facts.quote: The V. molyi specimen MLP-PV 93-I-5-1 displays pathological bone callus located on the mid-proximal portion of a rib, indicative of a fracture. Misalignment of the portions of the fractured rib occurred as it was healing.

facts.statement: Vegasaurus lived during the Maastrichtian stage, from 72.2 to 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Maastrichtian to Maastrichtian (72.2 to 66 million years ago)

rejected.quote: Vegasaurus is an extinct genus of elasmosaurid plesiosaur known from the Late Cretaceous (early Maastrichtian stage) Snow Hill Island Formation of Vega Island, Antarctic Peninsula.
